newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian government lashes out as protests continue.
newsitem.headline: Serbian government lashes out as protests continue.

text.p: The Serbian opposition continued demonstrations on Wednesday despite a law reversing election fraud that sparked the protests and in the face of concern that tensions could escalate.

Serbian parliament speaker Dragan Tomic slammed the opposition movement, saying the three months of protests were "violent and threatening" and adding "there is not one single reason for them to continue".
"These marches of groups of citizens in parts of the city appeared horrific," Tomic, one of the hardliners in President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialist party, told Radio Belgrade.
"It is not only a matter of disturbing citizens but of a kind of violence. Those shouts and cries must frighten any peaceful citizens."

Milosevic's Socialists caved in on Tuesday when parliament passed a law reinstating victories by the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition in 14 cities, including Belgrade, annulled for "irregularities" after November elections.

But Zajedno and their student allies, who fought the election fraud by mounting daily demonstrations for 12 weeks, said they would not let up the pressure for the government to make additional reforms.
The students' demands include the sacking of the Belgrade University rector and a student co-rector while one of Zajedno's demands is for greater access to strictly-controlled state media.

Some 15,000 students marched in Belgrade at mid-day on Wednesday and thousands of Zajedno supporters watched in the evening as a red boat, about 1.5 m (five-feet) long, was launched in the Danube River.
Demonstrators chanted "Out, Slobo (Milosevic), out" and sang "And Now Adio" as the boat symbolically carrying the Socialists "out to sea" was set adrift, to an accompanying display of fireworks.
"Communism has finally gone down the river and there is no communism in Serbia as of tonight," Zoran Djindjic, one of the co-leaders of Zajedno, told Reuters Television.
Djindjic was dismissive of the parliament speaker's comments saying, "He has said what we already know -- that Tomic is afraid of his own people.
"Every spontaneous gathering of people defending their rights appears to him as a threat...This shows how estranged from the people the authorities are and why these protests must take place at all."

The reinstatement of the Zajedno victories after three months of daily protests and widespread international condemnation of the Serbian government was welcomed with caution by Britain, France and Germany.
"This is an important step in the right direction. The law has been voted, now it must be applied," French foreign ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux told reporters in Paris.

Zajedno, often wrong-footed by the government in legal ploys over the November elections, was cautious about declaring the electoral battle over until Zajedno councillors are installed, which could take from three to 10 days.
Meanwhile the neo-communist Yugoslav United Left (JUL) party, a hardline ruling coalition partner, warned against moves to topple the government by the street protests.

"I don't understand, do they (opposition) expect the police and the state to do nothing in their defence?" Belgrade VIP newsletter quoted JUL spokesman Aleksandar Vulin as saying in an interview with Belgrade's Nedeljni Telegraf.
The West has cautioned Milosevic against using force on peaceful demonstrators and to open dialogue with his rivals, notably on the issues of access to the media.
In return Zajedno leaders are reported to have promised the West they would stop testing Milosevic's patience on the streets once their victories are reinstated.
